overview: Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Temple (Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Devasthanam), popularly known as Edupayala Temple, is one of the most revered Swayambhu Shakti temples in Telangana. Located at Nagasanpally village, Papannapet Mandal, Medak district, the temple sits in the middle of the Manjeera River, where it splits into seven distinct streams — hence the name 'Edupayala' (Telugu 'Edu' = seven, 'Payalu' = streams). Per some traditions, the seven streams are named after the seven great sages: Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama. The presiding deity is Goddess Vana Durga Bhavani (Edupayalamma), a forest-form of Goddess Durga who is believed to be self-manifested (Swayambhu) in a den ('Pedda Gutta Soramgam' / 'Garuda Ganga'). The complex is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department under a non-hereditary Trust Board, with A. Chandrasekhar as the Executive Officer. The annual Edupayala Jatara, celebrated around Maha Shivaratri (Feb/Mar), is a State Festival of Telangana and one of the state's largest religious gatherings. Every year ~30 lakh devotees visit; the three-day Jatara draws 5+ lakh pilgrims. During the monsoon, the seven swollen rivulets flow around and reach the feet of the Goddess — an event considered highly auspicious and at times severe enough to submerge the temple (as in August–October 2025, when the temple was underwater for 50+ days due to Singur dam releases).
summary: Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Temple at Nagasanpally, Papannapet Mandal, Medak District, Telangana, is a Swayambhu Shakti shrine dedicated to Goddess Vana Durga Bhavani (Edupayalamma). Believed established in the 12th century and administered by the Telangana Endowments Department under a non-hereditary Trust Board, it sits in the middle of the Manjeera River at the point where it splits into seven sacred streams (named after the seven sages). The annual Edupayala Jatara, held around Maha Shivaratri and Magha Amavasya, is a State Festival of Telangana. The temple draws ~30 lakh devotees annually; the three-day Jatara draws 5+ lakh pilgrims for Bonam offerings, Bandi Utsavam and Rathotsavam. It is recognised as the third-largest religious congregation in Telangana (after Sammakka-Sarakka Jatara and Peddagattu Jatara) per Wikipedia, but is also commonly described as the 'second-largest' by tourism sources.

history.content: The temple is believed to have been established in the 12th century and has remained an important centre of Shakti worship ever since. The presiding deity is Goddess Vana Durga (a forest form of Durga), who is believed to be self-manifested (Swayambhu) in a den (Pedda Gutta Soramgam, also called Garuda Ganga). A popular legend links the seven streams to the Mahabharata: King Janamejaya (son of Maharaja Parikshit, grandson of Arjuna) performed the Sarpa Yagna to avenge his father's death by snakebite. During the ritual, when Garuda carried away the sacrificial snakes, drops of their blood (per some versions) — or the spirit of Ganga (per other versions) — fell at seven different places, forming the seven streams that converge at Edupayala before joining the Manjeera River. Some traditions specifically name the streams after the seven great sages: Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama. Per temple tradition, the Goddess's idol was discovered in a den on the way to the temple, and the seven streams are said to touch the feet of the Goddess at the point where they merge.

history.content: Per the Wikipedia article on Papannapet, the temple's maintenance was under family members of Peddalachannagari's during the Nizam's rule. Peddalachannagai Durga Reddy was the first chairman of the temple Trust board. In 2015, the Telangana government constituted non-hereditary Trust Boards for 19 major temples under the AP Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act 1987 (Telangana Adaptation order 2014); Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Temple (Nagasanipally village, Papannapet Mandal, Medak District) was named as one of the 16 major temples with annual income above Rs 1 crore. The Edupayala Jatara was accorded the status of a State Festival. The current Executive Officer (as of 2025) is A. Chandrasekhar. In 2025, the temple was submerged for 50+ days due to heavy monsoon rain combined with massive releases from the Singur project (nearly one lakh cusecs); property loss was preliminarily estimated at ₹1 crore, and the Navaratri celebrations were held for the first time atop the flooded structure.

sthala_puranam: The place name 'Edupayala' comes from the Telugu 'Edu' (seven) and 'Payalu' (streams). Per the Mahabharata-linked legend, during King Janamejaya's Sarpa Yagna, Garuda carried away the sacrificial snakes, and drops of blood (or the spirit of Ganga, per other versions) fell at seven different places, forming the seven streams that converge at the temple before joining the Manjeera River. Per local tradition, the Goddess's idol was discovered in a den ('Pedda Gutta Soramgam' / 'Garuda Ganga') on the way to the temple, sanctifying the site for the manifestation of Goddess Vana Durga Bhavani. The seven streams are named after the seven great sages: Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama. During the monsoon, the rising waters of the Manjeera reach the feet of the Goddess — an event devotees consider highly auspicious.
religious_significance: Edupayala is regarded as one of the most powerful Shakti temples in Telangana. Goddess Vana Durga is worshipped as the divine protector who removes obstacles, grants courage, ensures prosperity, and safeguards families from negative influences. The seven sacred streams, in which pilgrims take a purifying holy bath before worship, are central to its spiritual importance. The temple is part of the Saptarishi tradition, with the seven streams named after the seven great sages.
spiritual_significance: The temple is especially sought for blessings of marriage, children, education, business and overall well-being, and for relief from hardships, marriage delays, health issues, financial difficulties and childlessness. Devotees believe a holy bath at the seven-stream confluence before prayers purifies body and mind. The annual Edupayala Jatara, Navaratri, Dasara and Bonalu are the most spiritually charged times to visit. The temple is one of three major Shakti temples in Telangana, alongside the others in the Jogulamba / Alampur tradition.

miracles_and_devotee_experiences: Devotees report prayers answered after offering Bonam, Kumkum Pooja and Abhishekam.

During monsoon, when Manjeera waters rise and touch the Goddess's feet, thousands consider it a miraculous, highly auspicious event.

architecture: The temple is uniquely situated in the middle of the Manjeera River, where it splits into seven distinct streams. The shrine sits in a den ('Pedda Gutta Soramgam' / 'Garuda Ganga') and blends naturally with its surroundings — dense teak and bamboo forests, rocky hills, and flowing water. It features a traditional entrance (Raja Gopuram), spacious prayer halls, mandapams, and a sanctum housing the Swayambhu idol of Sri Vana Durga Bhavani. The complex includes smaller shrines to Lord Shiva, Lord Ganesha and other deities. During monsoon the seven streams flow around the temple, creating a breathtaking (and at times flood-prone) landscape. Recent infrastructure includes improved pathways, bathing ghats, queue complexes, a prasadam distribution shed, a women's dressing shed, railings, and function-hall facilities for festival crowds. A 2025 flood (Singur releases) damaged the flooring, prasadam shed, women's dressing shed, railings, surrounding sheds, CCTV cameras, electric poles and power lines (preliminary loss estimate: ₹1 crore).

festivals.description: The temple's most important festival, celebrated around Maha Shivaratri and Magha Amavasya (Feb/Mar). Recognised as a State Festival of Telangana. The three-day festival begins on Shivaratri (Sunday), with Bandi Utsavam (procession of decorated bullock carts from 32 villages) on Monday and Rathotsavam on Tuesday. It draws 5+ lakh devotees for Bonam offerings, Panchamruta Abhishekam, Bandi Utsavam, Rathotsavam, cultural performances and special poojas. Per Wikipedia, Edupayala Jatara is the third-largest congregation in Telangana after Sammakka-Sarakka Jatara and Peddagattu Jatara (some tourism sources describe it as the second-largest).

A major Telangana festival celebrated at the temple during Ashada Masam (July–August). Women carry decorated pots (bonam) filled with food offerings to the Goddess, accompanied by drummers and devotees. The Bonalu Jatara is the temple's grandest folk celebration per Telangana360.

Nine-night festival celebrated with Kumkum Poojas, Chandi Homams and devotional programs. In 2025, for the first time, the Navaratri celebrations were held atop the flooded temple structure (due to Singur releases).

darshan_and_tickets.general_darshan: General darshan is free for all devotees (per Telangana360, edupayala.blogspot.com, and Deccan Chronicle's reportage). No advance online booking required.
darshan_and_tickets.special_darshan: Special pooja and seva tickets are available at the temple counter (charges not published in any verified source).
darshan_and_tickets.ticket_details: Offerings such as Abhishekam, Kumkum Archana, Chandi Homam and other rituals are performed on payment of prescribed seva charges (not publicly listed). Donations can be made for Annadanam and temple development. The temple is listed in the 2015 Telangana Trust Board notification as having annual income above Rs 1 crore, indicating a significant devotee/pooja flow.

dress_code: Devotees are encouraged to wear traditional and modest attire. Men generally wear dhoti, kurta or decent Indian clothing; women are advised to wear sarees, salwar kameez or other traditional dresses. Shorts, sleeveless tops and revealing outfits are discouraged. Footwear must be removed before entering, silence should be maintained in the sanctum, and photography may be restricted near the main deity.

accommodation.availability: Limited accommodation is available through the nearby Haritha Hotel (Telangana Tourism) and a few guest houses and lodges. Because the temple is in a forested region, many devotees stay in Medak (~19 km), Sangareddy or nearby towns, which offer a wider range of options. Temporary shelters and makeshift tents are arranged by devotees and the temple around the hillocks during the Jatara.
accommodation.booking_process: Advance booking is recommended for festivals and weekends, as accommodation fills quickly. No formal online booking for temple-managed accommodation.
accommodation.price_range: Haritha Hotel: Non-AC and AC rooms ~₹800–₹2,000 per night (per user doc; not independently verified on the Telangana Tourism portal in the sources reviewed). Private lodges in Medak and nearby towns: ~₹700–₹2,500 per night.

best_time_to_visit: October to March for pleasant weather (post-monsoon offers serene river views, clear access routes, and tranquil surroundings). Visit during the monsoon (July–September) to witness the seven streams at their fullest, when they swell and flow around the sanctum to the Goddess's feet — though access may be cut off during peak floods (as in Aug–Oct 2025). The Edupayala Jatara (around Maha Shivaratri and Magha Amavasya, Feb/Mar) and Bonalu Jatara (Ashada Masam, Jul–Aug) are the most spiritually charged times to visit. The 2025 Jatara was 6–8 March 2025.

travel.road: Approximately 110–120 km from Hyderabad (2.5–3 hours). Multiple routes: via Narsapur X Roads (Balanagar–Narsapur–Medak road, with an arch of the temple on the main road, then 7 km inside — per edupayala.blogspot.com); via NH 65 (Hyderabad–Nizamabad) to Medak (~90 km, 2 hours), then to Edupayala village (~40 km, 1 hour) per Telangana360. Connected by TSRTC and APSRTC (special buses during Jatara), private buses, taxis and private vehicles. The road passes through picturesque villages, teak/bamboo forests and agricultural fields. ~19 km from Medak town; ~12 km from Medak per edupayala.blogspot.com.
travel.rail: Nearest railway stations: Akkannapet (~19 km, per HinduPad) and Wadiaram; Kamareddy (~60 km, per HinduPad) is also a nearby major station. Medak is the nearest major town for transport and accommodation. Hyderabad is the nearest major railhead (per edupayala.blogspot.com).

introduction.en: Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Temple, popularly known as Edupayala Temple, is one of the most revered Swayambhu Shakti temples in Telangana. Located at Nagasanpally village, Papannapet Mandal, Medak district, about 110 to 120 kilometres from Hyderabad, it is dedicated to Goddess Vana Durga Bhavani, Edupayalamma. The name 'Edupayala' comes from the Telugu for seven streams, as the temple sits in the middle of the Manjeera River at the exact point where it splits into seven sacred streams named after the seven great sages. Set amid dense teak and bamboo forests, it draws around thirty lakh devotees annually and hosts the famous Edupayala Jatara around Maha Shivaratri, a State Festival of Telangana.

history.en: Believed established in the 12th century, the temple's presiding deity is a Swayambhu idol of Goddess Vana Durga discovered in a den called Pedda Gutta Soramgam or Garuda Ganga. Per the Mahabharata-linked legend, during King Janamejaya's Sarpa Yagna, Garuda carried away the sacrificial snakes, and drops of their blood (or the spirit of Ganga) fell at seven places, forming the seven streams that converge at the temple. Under the Nizam's rule, the temple was maintained by the Peddalachannagari family; in 2015, it was brought under a non-hereditary Trust Board of the Telangana Endowments Department, and the Edupayala Jatara was recognised as a State Festival.

travel_guide.en: Edupayala Temple is about 110 to 120 kilometres from Hyderabad, a two and a half to three hour drive. From Hyderabad, take the Balanagar–Narsapur–Medak road (an arch of the temple is on the main road, with the temple about 7 km inside), or NH 65 via Medak and then on to Papannapet. The nearest railway stations are Akkannapet, about 19 kilometres, and Kamareddy, about 60 kilometres. The nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad, about 140 to 146 kilometres. Darshan is generally 5:30 AM to 6:30 PM on weekdays and 5:00 AM to 7:00 PM on Sundays, though JustDial lists 6:00 AM to 6:00 PM daily. October to March is the best season; the Edupayala Jatara is in February or March, and the Bonalu Jatara is in July to August.

faq.question: Where is Sri Edupayala Vana Durga Bhavani Temple located?
faq.answer: The temple is located at Nagasanpally (also spelled Nagasanipally) Village, Papannapet Mandal, Medak District, Telangana — in the middle of the Manjeera River where it splits into seven streams. About 110–120 km from Hyderabad; ~19 km from Medak town.

faq.question: Which deity is worshipped in the temple?
faq.answer: The temple is dedicated to Goddess Sri Vana Durga Bhavani (Edupayalamma), a Swayambhu forest-form of Goddess Durga whose idol was discovered in a den called Pedda Gutta Soramgam (Garuda Ganga). Smaller shrines for Lord Shiva and Lord Ganesha are also present.

faq.question: Why is Edupayala Temple famous?
faq.answer: It is famous for being located at the confluence of seven streams of the Manjeera River (the seven streams are named after the seven great sages — Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama). The annual Edupayala Jatara (around Maha Shivaratri and Magha Amavasya) is a State Festival of Telangana and one of the state's largest religious gatherings, drawing 5+ lakh devotees over three days and ~30 lakh annually.

faq.question: What are the temple timings?
faq.answer: Most sources agree on 5:30 AM–6:30 PM Monday–Saturday and 5:00 AM–7:00 PM Sunday (HinduPad). JustDial's listing (Naganpally, 502287) gives 6:00 AM–6:00 PM daily; Telangana360 gives 6:00 AM–7:00 PM daily. Hours are extended during the Edupayala Jatara, Maha Shivaratri, Navaratri, Dasara and Bonalu. During severe floods (e.g. Aug–Oct 2025), the temple was closed and rituals shifted to the Raja Gopuram or function hall.

faq.question: Is there an entry fee for darshan?
faq.answer: No. General darshan is free for all devotees (per Telangana360, edupayala.blogspot.com, and Deccan Chronicle's reportage). Charges apply only for special poojas and sevas (specific tariff not publicly listed).

faq.question: Which is the biggest festival celebrated here?
faq.answer: Two main festivals: the Edupayala Jatara (Maha Shivaratri / Magha Amavasya, Feb/Mar) — a State Festival of Telangana with Panchamruta Abhishekam, Bandi Utsavam and Rathotsavam — and the Bonalu Jatara (Ashada Masam, Jul–Aug). Per Wikipedia, Edupayala Jatara is the third-largest religious congregation in Telangana after Sammakka-Sarakka Jatara and Peddagattu Jatara (some tourism sources call it the second-largest).

faq.question: Are accommodation facilities available near the temple?
faq.answer: Limited — the Haritha Hotel (Telangana Tourism) is the closest named option (verify on the Telangana Tourism portal), plus private hotels and lodges in Medak (~19 km), Sangareddy (~65 km) and Kamareddy (~60 km). During the Jatara, devotees pitch makeshift tents around the hillocks.

faq.question: What is the best time to visit Edupayala Temple?
faq.answer: October to March for pleasant weather and post-monsoon serenity; February–March for the Edupayala Jatara; July–August for Bonalu and the spectacle of the swollen seven streams (though access may be cut off in heavy floods). The 2025 Jatara was 6–8 March 2025.

faq.question: What are the seven streams of Edupayala, and what do they represent?
faq.answer: The seven streams are named after the seven great sages (Saptarishis): Jamadagni, Atri, Kasyapa, Viswamitra, Vasistha, Bharadwaja and Gautama. They begin their journey from the Ghanpur project and meet just behind the sanctum, where the Goddess is enshrined. The place name 'Edupayala' means 'Seven Streams' in Telugu.

faq.question: Who administers the temple, and what is the contact?
faq.answer: The temple is administered by the Telangana Endowments Department under a non-hereditary Trust Board (constituted in 2015 as one of 19 major temples with annual income above ₹1 crore). The Executive Officer (as of 2025) is A. Chandrasekhar. Phone: +91-98663 31529 (per user doc) or +91-8452-222222 (Medak district Endowments office, per Telangana360). Email: eo.edupayala@endowments.telangana.gov.in (per user doc; standard EO email pattern).

faq.question: Is the Edupayala temple accessible for wheelchair users?
faq.answer: Yes, per JustDial the Edupayala Vana Durgamma Temple has 'Wheel Chair Accessible Entrance and Exit' amenities. However, the temple sits in the middle of the Manjeera River in a forested, rocky area with natural pathways, and accessibility may be limited during monsoon floods (as in Aug–Oct 2025 when the temple was submerged).
